content:
Hi all. On the (long) journey to Minkowski's Second Theorem, I started formalizing Michael's Selection Theorem. This states that a correspondence f : α → Set β from a normal, paracompact topological space α to a Frechet space β that is lower hemicontinuous, and has nonempty, closed, convex values admits a continuous selection, i.e., a map g : α → β such that g x ∈ f x for all x.

Currently, correspondences primarily show up in mathlib's definition of hemicontinuity, see here and are notated as α → Set β.

However, correspondences have slightly different semantics that typical maps. For instance, the graph of a correspondence is {x : α × β | x.2 ∈ f x.1} and whether this graph is open or closed often shows up as a condition in major theorems (e.g., Kakutani's Fixed Point theorem demands the graph be closed).

@Jireh Loreaux #38600 that mathlib consider adding an abbrev Set.Correspondence meaning the type α → Set β and a piece of notation, e.g., α ⇉ β, which matches the literature. This would allow creating definitions like Set.Correspondence.graph instead of the more awkward CGraph constructions in #38600.

Some considerations:

* Different fields give this object different names. For instance, economics calls this a "set-valued function"
* There are already things called "correspondence" in mathlib, e.g., Setoid.correspondence and related objects in group theory
* In category theory, there's a more general notion of a "span," i.e., a pair of arrows X ← Γ → Y. A set-valued function is a span in the category of sets where the map Γ → X is surjective and the associated map Γ → X ×ˢ Y is injective. This theory gives you nice properties like a natural definition of composition of spans (when the underlying category has pullbacks) and has wide applications such as Hecke correspondences.

For my work, I basically just need the definition for Set, and so I'd propose creating Set.Correspondence, but I was curious what the overall community sentiment was before implementing such a change.

@Jireh Loreaux as there's not been much discussion here, re #38600, there are a couple paths forward:

  1. The Set.Correspondence abbreviation and namespace can be created and _all_ the hemicontinuous notions be migrated into that space;
  2. Same, but only the notion of graph and comp can be implemented in the namespace, with the rest of the notions being external; or
  3. Keep as is

I would suggest (1). In which case, I would:

  • First create a PR moving everything that is currently in master to the Set.Correspondence namespace. (I don't quite know how to deprecate in this case. I would love a pointer on this.)
  • Then rebase #38600 on top of that, moving the notions into the namespace.

Happy to create that PR if no one is opposed :-)
Isn't this kind of like docs#SetRel ?
Right, SetRel A B, Correspondence A B and Rel A B are all trivially isomorphic, and it's not clear to me that #38600 merits introducing the third way of spelling things

Make sense! I was looking at the hemicontinuity definitions and not paying attention to SetRel.

Out of curiosity, @Jireh Loreaux was there a reason to frame hemicontinuity in terms of maps α → Set β instead of as a property of SetRel 's? If it makes more sense, I could refactor the hemicontinuity results to be stated in terms of SetRel

Well, certainly one reason is that α → Set β is the way hemicontinuity is usually expressed in the literature, and moreover the only (current) use case for hemicontinuity in Mathlib pertains to docs#upperHemicontinuous_spectrum (this is used in rather important ways to prove continuity results for docs#cfc, such as docs#Continuous.cfc_of_mem_nhdsSet, which in turn is used to prove docs#CFC.continuous_abs, among other things), and spectrum R : A → Set R fits this paradigm. To fit this into the docs#Rel framework, one would have to consider fun a r ↦ r ∈ spectrum R a : Rel A R. This is not a deal-breaker, but I wouldn't prefer it.

I agree that most of the literature I see refers to “set valued functions” and not relations. My use case was selection theorems, where you have to insist on things like “the value at every point is closed and convex” and my primary use case is when the correspondence is the inverse relation of a function. The latter already fits into the SetRel framework, but the former is a bit awkward.

Perhaps the missing component an easy way to write ‘f a = { b : r a b}’? It might exist in docs#SetRel but I couldn’t find it.

(FWIW, with a few hints Claude could vibe code a refactor to defining Lower Hemicontinuity in terms of ‘fun x t => IsOpen t \and x \in f.preimage t’ where f is a SetRel in Defs.lean, but I haven’t tried Upper Hemicontinuity and the downstream files)
docs#SetRel.image ?
It's not clear to me that SetRel is better here than using raw relations

On docs#SetRel.image the only downside is that you end up having to wrap all your inputs as sets, eg, f.image {x} so it’s a little awkward as people who think about “set valued functions” would generally want to spell it as ‘f x’

One advantage of SetRel is that a common condition for selection and related theorems is that the graph of the correspondence be open or closed. And for a SetRel the graph itself is the object. But you could also do it with a Rel.
Yeah, I certainly wouldn't go fornSetRel for hemi continuity, but a bare relation could be reasonable, even if it's maybe not ideal in that it doesn't match the literature.

I still am not super familiar with why you might style things one way over another, so this may be a silly suggestion: if you add a CoeFun instance to SetRel yields the set-valued function associated with the SetRel then would that bridge the gap in notation?

OK, I got a chance to look at SetRel a bit more, and some notes. If you take f : SetRel A B then you do get some nice things falling out of the API, e.g.,

(1) Upper hemicontinuity is essentially a statement about cores, specifically:

lemma upperHemicontinuous_iff_isOpen_core :
    UpperHemicontinuous f ↔ ∀ u, IsOpen u → IsOpen (f.core u) := sorry

(2) Open and closed graphs are just IsOpen f and IsClosed f.

(3) Statements like "A map g is open if and only if its inverse relation is lower hemicontinuous" becomes:

lemma isOpenMap_iff_graph_inv_lowerHemicontinuous (g : A → B) :
    IsOpenMap g ↔ LowerHemicontinuous (Function.graph g).inv

(4) Composition works nicely. Specifically, if f and g are hemicontinuous / have open graphs / etc, then so does f ○ g

Of course, this is really just saying that the SetRel API is nice.

Some parts of the SetRel API exist elsewhere, e.g., Relation.Comp exists. I wonder if the "correct" thing here would be to implement a few more Relation notions (such as Core)?

Kevin Wilson said:

Some parts of the SetRel API exist elsewhere, e.g., Relation.Comp exists. I wonder if the "correct" thing here would be to implement a few more Relation notions (such as Core)?

In CSLib I am working through the same question, as we also inherit uses of unbundled relations from core and Mathlib applied to topics like lambda calculi or reductions more generally. For instance, I recently found myself wanting SetRel.{cod,dom} for unbundled relations and broadly find it awkward to talk about the restriction of an unbundled relation (see #CSLib > unbundled relations with restricted (co)domain). If this sort of work is useful to Mathlib, I am happy to help out.

Based on the above, it seems like there are a few choices:

Create a "unbundled" version of the SetRel API

Upsides: provides a lot of useful notions (graphs, composition, inversion, etc.) currently only available through the SetRel API. Would be helpful for parts of CSLib as @Chris Henson mentions. Some parts already exist (e.g., Relation.Comp)

Downsides: A lot of duplication between Rel and SetRel unless there's a clever way to package.

For hemicontinuity: Define hemicontinuity for Rel's and modify the downstream proofs.

Define Hemicontinuity in terms of SetRel

Upsides: No new code or duplication. The API dovetails very nicely with the notion of hemicontinuity (see above).

Downsides: Not really natural (either from the literature or from likely usage for proving things like selection theorems and fixed point theorems). Also wouldn't really solve the problem that @Chris Henson is pointing out about bare Rels and wanting to use them elsewhere.

For hemicontinuity: Would define in terms of SetRel. See above for some examples of how this would look.

Ignore the problem for now

Upsides: Nothing to be done :-)

Downsides: To prove facts like Michael's selection theorem, you really need to introduce a bunch of notions like the graph of a set-valued function to declare it to be open. So you end up defining much of the API you'd build for an unbundled Rel anyway, but maybe not in the optimal way.

For hemicontinuity: Would continue to define in terms of "set valued functions" and would define, at least, lower sections and "correspondence graphs" as in #38600.

Question

Is there a reasonable way to resolve this problem? I'm happy to implement any of the above (especially if Chris wants to help!), but would love to close out at least the selection theorem PR (so that I can eventually merge in the minkowski's second theorem things :-) )
Perhaps of interest that there used to be an "unbundled" relation API, and @Yaël Dillies recently replaced it with the SetRel API
What's the statement of Michael's selection theorem under the "do nothing" proposal?
See #39116

Eric Wieser said:

Perhaps of interest that there used to be an "unbundled" relation API, and Yaël Dillies recently replaced it with the SetRel API

Yes, I guess my earlier comment is a bit unproductive in suggesting the opposite of this (#25587) without much careful thought. My question is more about working with for instance docs#Relation.TransGen, docs#Relation.ReflTransGen, etc. that is maybe a bit separate from this discussion.

Kevin Wilson said:

See #39116

CI is failing on that PR becaause you haven't run lake exe mk_all
(and then it will fail because docs#HasOpenLowerSections doesn't exist)

But either way, I think the existing statement looks fine, and the process should be:

  • Get that PR through review without introducing Set.Correspondence or using SetRel
  • Only then evaluate whether a switch to one or the other is worth it; this is much easier to evaluate in the form of a PR presenting a diff between the "do nothing" and "do something" option
Sounds good! I have made an update to #38600 and then will work through #38601 (which contains docs#HasOpenLowerSections) and other dependent PRs
If folks are interested, #38601 is now merged and so #39116 (the actual statement of Michael's selection theorem) is ready for review. :-)
